Conclusion
As both a market and an institution the London Stock Exchange occupied a central position within the British ﬁnancial
system. As Britain was such a key component of the world economy from 1700 the result was to make the London
Stock Exchange central to the operation of the international ﬁnancial system, for much of the period. Thus, in dealing
with the history of the London Stock Exchange one is examining an institution of immense importance and inﬂuence.
Unfortunately, the role it performed went largely unrecognized by both contemporaries and later historians. The
raising of capital for governments and business is largely attributed to those who actively mobilized the funds, such as
the investment banks, with little comprehension of the role played by the existence of a market where the resulting
securities could be traded. The provision of the credit required by industry and trade is attributed to the commercial
banks, who collected and lent the savings of the nation. There is limited understanding of how the existence of
transferable securities and an organized market blurred the distinctions between the short- and long-term use of such
funds. The successful operation of an international monetary system before 1914, and its collapse and its
reconstruction thereafter, is identiﬁed with the functioning of the gold standard and the guiding inﬂuence of central
banks and not the presence of an exchange where the international ownership of assets could be traded. Throughout
its history the prime function of the London Stock Exchange, as an organized market for existing securities, has been
downplayed because of its association with speculation. Instead of trying to investigate the causes and consequences of
this constant buying and selling, the assumption is made that, because it is rooted in the individual's desire to sell—not
produce—for a proﬁt, it does not perform a function within the wider economy. Consequently, the existence of the
London Stock Exchange can only be justiﬁed by attributing to it the activities of others, such as those issuing securities
and the use government and business made of the ﬁnance so obtained.
At the same time there is a tendency to see the entire period, until the more recent past, as one when markets, of
whatever kind, operated autonomously. Markets were neither organized nor regulated by governments but left to the
free operation of Adam Smith's hidden hand, through
                                                     CONCLUSION                                                      637


which equilibrium was maintained by competing forces of supply and demand. Eventually this broke down in the
twentieth century and the state had to intervene. Under this scenario there is no recognition that these markets were by
no means unmanaged. The very development of exchanges, whether stock or commodity, as well as a proliferation of
trade and other business associations and bodies, testiﬁed to the need for organization and regulation, and the ready
response from those directly involved. The era before 1939 was one not so much of laissez-faire but self-regulation, in
which the government laid down the law of the land, leaving the organization to monitor and police the behaviour of
their own members. In increasingly complex and interdependent economies the forces of supply and demand had to
be modiﬁed so as to ensure the speedy completion of transactions. It was not simply price that had to be determined,
but the amount, the quality, and the timing and location of delivery. All that required a great deal of trust between the
participants, ranging all the way from the original producer and ﬁnal consumer through the intermediaries involved.
Once an economy moved away from a position of the production of a few basic goods for immediate consumption, as
in a subsistence culture, systems were essential to guarantee that bargains made would be adhered to. The more
complex and sophisticated the economy the more complex and sophisticated the systems in place needed to be. The
motto of the London Stock Exchange—‘My Word is My Bond’—could only be true in an organized and regulated
market, where failure to honour a sale or purchase could and did result in a ﬁne, suspension, or expulsion. In studying
the history of the London Stock Exchange one is examining how the world's ﬁrst modern economy coped with the
need not only to develop sophisticated securities markets in a technical sense but also to devise the institutional
mechanisms that facilitated their operation. Both factors are of vital importance in explaining what took place,
assessing the results, and relating the outcome to the performance of both the British and world economies in those
years. Conversely, in the years after the Second World War the state became increasingly involved in the direction and
management of the securities market as the London Stock Exchange became a quasi-ofﬁcial arm of the government.
This in turn had major consequences for its operation and the role it was able to play both domestically and
internationally.
The history of the London Stock Exchange, divides into ﬁve distinct periods. The ﬁrst begins in the late seventeenth
century and culminates in the mid-1820s. During those years the Stock Exchange emerged as a distinct entity within
the securities market, providing an organized forum for the trading of mainly UK government debt rather than
corporate stocks and bonds. Covering the period from the mid-1820s until the First World War, the second period sees
the London Stock Exchange emerge as one of the central institutions of both the British and the world economy.
Expanding
638                                                    CONCLUSION


beyond its initial focus on the National Debt the London Stock Exchange increasingly provided a market for both
domestic and foreign corporate stocks and bonds. Probably no single Stock Exchange ever provided a market for such
a large proportion of the world's securities as London did at this time. However, this market did more than facilitate
the mobilization of long-term capital for the development of the world economy. It also imparted liquidity and
mobility to the monetary systems of the world, creating an integrated global economy in the process. The third period
covered an era from the beginning of the First World War in 1914 to the start of another in 1939, with the virtual
collapse of the international economy in between. Within the space of those 25 years, the achievements of the past two
centuries were largely lost or reversed. The London Stock Exchange was returned to a position where the National
Debt dominated trading, and its precise relations to the money and capital markets were uncertain. On the eve of the
Second World War it was not at all clear what the future held for the London Stock Exchange. In the fourth period,
covering the years from the Second World War until the 1980s the London Stock Exchange retreated almost entirely
from its international role. Instead, it found a new role for itself as the semi-ofﬁcial regulator of the domestic securities
market. This was a position it used to safeguard the interests of its members against competition. The ﬁnal period
began in the 1970s and is still continuing today. After appearing to consolidate its control over the domestic securities
market, by merging with the provincial stock exchanges in 1973, the London Stock Exchange gradually lost the role it
had gained after the Second World War. Attacks by the government on restrictive practices, criticism from the rest of
the City for its charges and practices, and growing competition from non-members aided by rapid changes in
communications and the ending of exchange controls, left the Stock Exchange without the support it required to resist
change. When that came with Big Bang in 1986 it began a process of transformation that nobody envisaged, few
wanted, and none could stop. The only certainty remaining for the London Stock Exchange, as it approached its third
century, was that it only had a future if it changed, but then it had done precisely that over two centuries. In the
eighteenth century the London securities market had no formal organization and concerned itself with dealing in UK
government debt, or proxies for, with most of the activity driven by the short-term considerations of the money
market. In the late twentieth century the London Stock Exchange was a highly organized market place for the stocks
and shares of British and foreign companies, with most activity driven by the short- and long-term interests of
institutional investors.
This story of change has the appeal of simplicity and an air of inevitability but the reality was much more complex than
that. Though the securities market that was developing in London in the eighteenth century did grow in size and
sophistication, it remained inferior to Amsterdam. Instead
                                                      CONCLUSION                                                      639


of a gradual overtaking of Amsterdam, to become the leading securities market in Europe, it was the upheavals of
revolution and war that were instrumental in London's success. The switch of ﬁnancial leadership away from
Amsterdam and to London owed more to the political, military, and economic misfortunes of continental Europe
between 1789 and 1815 than to the growing economic power of an industrializing Britain. The London Stock
Exchange's connection with the ﬁnance of economic growth at that stage remained tenuous in the extreme, and it
could thus not expect to proﬁt greatly from the process at so early a stage. Conversely, the rise to world importance of
the London Stock Exchange during the nineteenth century did owe much to the growing wealth and prosperity of
Britain. The accumulation of savings and its mobilization for investment, created a need for a ﬁnancial institution like
the London Stock Exchange. In turn, the facilities it provided were increasingly tapped by savers and borrowers
worldwide, as investors, governments, and business recognized the merits of securities as either attractive investments
or cheap ﬁnance. By responding to this merging global market, through a liberal policy on the admission of members,
the quotation of securities, and the degree of regulation the London Stock Exchange became one of the key
institutions of the world's capitalist economy.
On the eve of the First World War there seemed nothing that could stop the onward march of securities and the stock
exchanges on which they were traded, with London being the greatest of all. Even the war itself, with its vast increase
in transferable debt in order to ﬁnance such an intense and prolonged conﬂict, should only have enhanced the position
of the London Stock Exchange. However, what had been ignored was the fact that the securities market could only
prosper and thrive under conditions of trust and stability. The purchase of a transferable security was, itself, an act of
faith in the existence of a guaranteed future income and the ability to resell as and when required. It had taken years to
build up conﬁdence in the safety and marketability of securities, to a level where long-term debt was used for
employing short-term money remuneratively and moving it around the world. Unfortunately, it was this conﬁdence
that was most affected by the First World War, and subsequent events, such as hyperinﬂation in Germany, the Wall
Street crash, the collapse of monetary and ﬁnancial systems worldwide, the imposition of exchange controls, and the
repudiation of sovereign debts. Stock Exchanges were integral parts of national and global ﬁnancial systems and so
could not escape from the problems that affected them during and after the First World War. The London Stock
Exchange withstood the shocks better than most but even it was forced to accept a much changed and reduced role
for itself.
Thus, when the Second World War ended much of the trust and conﬁ-dence that had underpinned the growing use of
transferable securities and the free operation of markets had gone. Instead the power of government
640                                                  CONCLUSION


to direct, regulate, manage, and control had now become the central belief, to a greater or lesser extent, all round the
world. Within this new climate all the London Stock Exchange could do was to co-operate and survive, which it did.
However, in the process it gradually lost sense of the purpose for which it existed, which was the provision of an
orderly and dynamic market for transferable securities. When the demand for such a market did begin to revive slowly
in the 1950s the London Stock Exchange's response was a limited and tardy one, which was only partially due to the
restricted environment within which it was able to operate. Though response and change took place it was insufﬁcient
for the London Stock Exchange to capture the opportunities that were available to it, especially with the City of
London's re-emergence as a global ﬁnancial centre from the 1960s. Even when the Stock Exchange experienced a
period of rapid but belated change in the 1980s it was only sufﬁcient for it to recover some of the position it had once
occupied. To re-establish itself as one of the central institutions of a re-emerging global capitalist economy the London
Stock Exchange required to recapture the openness, responsiveness, and blend of liberality and regulation that had
characterized it before the First World War.
The institutional form that the London Stock Exchange took inﬂuenced its ability to respond to change. As long as
control of the Stock Exchange was divided between members and proprietors, then it operated as a dynamic, open
institution, and this was the case throughout the nineteenth century. Conversely, once control of the Stock Exchange
fell into the hands of the membership, as was the case between the wars, it became much more resistant to change,
though this took time to manifest itself. The real change came in 1947 when the members bought out the proprietors
and took control of the Exchange themselves. From then on they were answerable only to themselves for their actions,
and so could devise rules and regulations regarding such areas as admissions, number of members, scale of charges,
and ways of operating that were to their particular beneﬁt rather than in the interests of the securities market as a
whole. This might not have been particularly serious because competition within the securities market would have
limited their ability to abuse the power at their disposal. There were always alternative ways of trading securities and
the London Stock Exchange and its membership had no monopoly. Unfortunately this was also a time of greatly
increased government controls. Internationally the maintenance of exchange controls until 1979 insulated the London
Stock Exchange from external competition. Domestically, the use of the London Stock Exchange by the government,
through the Bank of England, as the means through which the securities market was controlled and policed, gave it
immense power to both neutralize competition and impose its own rules and regulations. In many ways Big Bang was
all about the end to that abuse of power by the Stock Exchange whose source had been government itself since 1945.
                                                       CONCLUSION                                                        641


A stock exchange like London's needs to discover an evolving compromise between regulation and freedom if it is to
be successful both as a market and an institution. Both elements were and are essential in the creation of an orderly and
dynamic market place. This had been achieved by the London Stock Exchange before the First World War and it was
this that was lost after the Second World War. Though the Stock Exchange itself, and its membership, have to bear
some responsibility for this loss, due attention must be paid to the environment within which they operated
throughout their existence. The period before 1914 was one of fairly liberal, open economies where government
intervention was limited both domestically and internationally. Thus the London Stock Exchange could ﬂourish as a
market place serving a global economy. The years after 1945 were quite the reverse of that, with government control
being experienced by all economies at all levels around the world. This created conditions where the existence of a
market like the London Stock Exchange was threatened, encouraging its membership to adopt strategies that would
safeguard their institution and their incomes. This they did successfully and it is against that they should be judged. In
retrospect it is now clear that the inﬂuence of government on the post-war development of the London Stock
Exchange was not a positive one. By creating a safe niche for the members of the London Stock Exchange in the
domestic securities market the government discouraged them, both individually and collectively, from seizing the
opportunities when they did emerge. Government control converted the London Stock Exchange from being a
dynamic element in the world economy to a conservative element within the domestic economy. Possibly this explains
much about the performance of the British economy in these post-war years if the pattern experienced by the London
Stock Exchange is repeated in other institutions and businesses. Only when the London Stock Exchange faced these
new challenges in the 1980s did it re-emerge as a more dynamic institution capable of formulating its own destiny
rather than being driven by the dictates of government and the activities of non-members.
If current trends are any indicator of future requirements there is every possibility of the London Stock Exchange
recapturing part of the role it had once occupied on the eve of the First World War. However, it can only do that if it
shows itself to be equally open and responsive as it was at that time. The status quo is no longer an option considering
the enormous changes taking place, unless the London Stock Exchange and its membership ﬁnd relegation to the role
of a local or regional market place particularly attractive. In contrast, the central position in the global market place has
not yet been ﬁlled and an obvious candidate is the stock exchange located in the City of London, considering the
concentration of money and capital market activity there. However, there is no necessity that such a market needs to be
located in London, considering modern communications, nor any guarantee that the London Stock Exchange would
ﬁll that
642                                                 CONCLUSION


role if it were, considering the existence of a separate Eurobond market. What is clear is that an orderly and dynamic
market is a necessity for the international securities business, whether involving equities and bonds, and that neither
governments nor central banks are suited to provide, control, or manage it. The history of the London Stock
Exchange suggests that self-regulation without monopoly power has produced the most satisfactory solution in the past.
Otherwise governments operate to their own agendas, distorting the market and destroying innovation in the process,
while self-regulating monopolies abuse their power for their own self-interest.
                                        EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY                                                 643


Epilogue: Towards a Third Century
Apart from the period immediately following the end of the Second World War, those directing the affairs of the
London Stock Exchange have never before been faced with such pressing and difﬁcult decisions regarding its future as
they are now, at the start of the twenty-ﬁrst century. In the short run, the decisions taken are likely to determine the
survival of those running the Stock Exchange, as the resignation of the Chief Executive, Gavin Casey, in September
2000 showed. More importantly, in the long run, the whole direction and future role of the London Stock Exchange is
dependent upon these decisions. That is not to say that the London Stock Exchange has not had to change in the past.
Its very survival over the last two centuries is testimony to the fact that those guiding the Stock Exchange's destiny
were able to respond to the challenges it faced and so continually reposition it in terms of the functions undertaken
and the role performed. In the ﬁrst century of the Stock Exchange's existence, this process of change was driven by
the needs of the marketplace—more investors, more securities, more members, more activity—and the increasingly
global nature of ﬁnance. Such was the success of the London Stock Exchange in its ﬁrst century that it dominated the
international securities market on the eve of the First World War. In the years after that war, and especially after the
Second World War, the wishes of the British government became paramount and it was to those that the Stock
Exchange had to respond and adjust if it was to survive. To secure a future for itself, those running the Stock
Exchange turned it into the semi-ofﬁcial regulator of the British securities market, standing between the government
of the day and those whose business it was to buy and sell stocks and shares. In retrospect that was an untenable
position, as the Stock Exchange was undertaking an ofﬁcial role without ofﬁcial sanction while, simultaneously,
carrying out its traditional function of providing an orderly market for all participants. It also led it to neglect the global
market where it had been so successful in the past. The ending of foreign exchange controls in 1979, leading to Big
Bang in 1986, brought to a close that era of the Stock Exchange's existence. In its place came the combination of an
increasingly competitive global marketplace and an increasingly interventionist, regulatory regime, and it is to these
forces that the Stock Exchange has to respond if it is to survive and prosper.
Since the 1980s, the London Stock Exchange has had to rediscover its traditional role as an organized marketplace
without the general regulatory functions that had allowed it to differentiate itself from other providers of trading
forums. Two of the last remaining statutory functions still
644                                    EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY


performed by the Stock Exchange were lost in 2000, namely the vetting of all public equity issues in the UK, and the
public disclosure of price-sensitive information. These would now be handled by the Financial Services Authority, with
its 2000 staff, in the same way as it had taken responsibility away from the Stock Exchange in so many other areas.
Nevertheless, the government continued to treat the Stock Exchange as some kind of semi-ofﬁcial body and so use it
as a tool of policy. For example, the Stock Exchange was expected to ensure that all companies whose shares it listed,
followed a particular code of corporate behaviour, even though this might make it less attractive to companies seeking
a quotation. Similarly, the Stock Exchange continued to be placed in an impossible position by the government with
regard to the listing of securities. If it was too lax and gave a market to high-risk companies without a track record of
proﬁtability and proven assets, then it would be condemned for not protecting the interests of investors. If it adopted a
more cautious approach and only accepted those companies that were tried and tested, then it would be condemned
for failing to back new and promising developments in the economy. Did the dot.com boom represent the Stock
Exchange at its best, by responding to the wishes of investors and entrepreneurs, or at its worst, by pandering to the
cravings of speculators and making it easy to ﬂoat dubious companies? As with all speculative booms, both elements
were present and government must recognize that it is not possible to legislate away ﬁnancial risk-taking without also
destroying the beneﬁts it brings. What should be recognized is that the Stock Exchange is there to provide a market
that is as fair and organized as possible, not to protect people from their own folly. Without the market that the Stock
Exchange provides, those companies which do eventually emerge as survivors from the dot.com mania would not
have been given that chance in the ﬁrst place. Out of the railway mania in the 1840s came a transport system that
revolutionized not only the British economy, but also that of the world, but in its wake there were numerous ruined
investors and abandoned projects. Such has been the inevitable outcome of all speculative booms, in all countries, at all
times, and in all ﬁelds.
The government also continued to regard the Stock Exchange as a simple and easy source of tax revenue through the
levy of stamp duty, regardless of the consequences this had upon London's ability to compete with markets elsewhere.
Stamp duty generated over £2 billion for the government in 1999, but, at 0.5 per cent of the value of a transaction, it
was set at one of the highest rates in the world. Many countries, such as Germany, had no such tax. In the past when
the level of other charges in London was high, as with broker commissions before Big Bang, stamp duty was less of a
burden. However, with competition and efﬁciency driving down all other charges, stamp duty became a
proportionately greater burden. Although the government was aware that it was increasingly easy to complete deals
                                       EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY                                               645


abroad through electronic links, it was unwilling to forgo this direct source of revenue in return for greater but indirect
gains through an increase in the number and income of those employed in securities dealing. Over time, the effects of
stamp duty will be to encourage companies to have their securities quoted on another market and for ﬁnancial
intermediaries to complete sales and purchases abroad, with detrimental consequences for the London securities
market in terms of the range and depth of turnover. As with other British industries, tax and regulatory regimes that
place those operating from a British base at a disadvantage will, eventually, drive business abroad, irrespective of the
underlying competitive position. The development of electronic communication networks has the power either to
bring business to London from all over the world, or to redirect British business abroad. What the result is to be will
depend on the relative service provided and the charges made, within which national taxation and legislation will be an
important inﬂuence.
Nevertheless, the role of government, whether British or European, was only one of the inﬂuences on the success or
otherwise of the Stock Exchange, as no major market was free of intervention, control, charges, and regulation. Freed
from the need to operate as the regulatory body for the securities industry, the London Stock Exchange had to become
much more responsive to the needs of those operating in the market if it was to maintain its role as a central
marketplace. However, it was restricted in its actions by the mutual nature of its organization. The problem with
mutuality was that it gave an equal voice to all members, no matter how much business they did or its particular nature.
Thus, the majority could, if they wished, prevent changes that would help reposition the Stock Exchange in the
marketplace if it was not to their speciﬁc and immediate interest. In 1999, for instance, out of the Stock Exchange's
298 members some 20 per cent were responsible for 80 per cent of the value of business done, and these largely
comprised a small number of American and European ﬁrms operating internationally. In contrast, around 100 of the
member ﬁrms did a largely British business on behalf of individual investors, with much being undertaken outside
London. In January 2000, the decision was taken to convert the Stock Exchange into a company in the belief that such
a change would make it easier to take decisions that might be at variance with the interests of many users, but that
better reﬂected the overall business being conducted. This was a move being followed by exchanges all around the
world for much the same reasons. Mutuality worked well in static situations where it was important to satisfy the
interests of all participants through a compromise solution, but it did not work well in rapidly changing environments
which demanded quick responses and involved both winners and losers. Thus, like many forms of business
organization, it suited particular situations at particular times, but was neither a permanent nor a universal solution.
Prior to 1947, one element of the Stock Exchange—the
646                                   EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY


buildings and the facilities it provided—had operated as a quoted public company that generated a proﬁt for its
shareholders. The other element—the rules governing the trading of securities—operated as a club, but not one with
any monopoly position, for a rival club could be formed. What happened in 1947 was that these two functions were
fused and then given a quasi-monopoly, so eliminating the competitive spur to change coming from either inside or
out. That is now changing again as distinct components of the securities industry are served by separate organizations:
the Securities Institute as the professional body, the FSA as the regulatory authority, and the Stock Exchange as the
market.
As a company, the London Stock Exchange gains the freedom to operate as a business in its own right, including
merging with stock exchanges in other countries, rather than conﬁning its horizons to activity in the London market or
Britain. Driving this move away from mutuality was the accelerating global nature of the securities market, inﬂuenced
by such factors as monetary integration and the convergence of information and communications technology. Lagging
behind these fundamental changes were attempts to create more integrated securities markets. National stock
exchanges had evolved to meet national needs and so their patterns of ownership, membership, trading systems, rules
and regulations, and even opening hours, all differed in numerous ways. This created near insuperable barriers to
achieving harmonization, let alone a common trading platform. It took years—even decades—of negotiation before
all the separate British stock exchanges united to form one single institution, and that was within one country with one
monetary system. Even then tensions and differences remained within the single organization. Consequently, it was no
surprise that the alliance of major European stock exchanges, proposed in 1998, had faltered and died by September
1999, although moves towards a gradual harmonization of national practices, such as the time taken to complete deals,
continued. Instead, what took its place were a series of proposed mergers between stock exchanges, as each sought to
secure a future for itself in an increasingly competitive world (e.g. the Scandinavian stock exchanges).
In particular, the Deutsche Börse tried to exploit indecision in the London Stock Exchange about its future and so
make Frankfurt the centre of the European securities market. In response, this led to an alliance between the Paris,
Amsterdam, and Brussels stock exchanges in March 2000, to be called Euronext. The aim of this combination was to
challenge both London and Frankfurt in Europe, and the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq globally. Paris was
to become the market for major company stocks, Brussels for smaller companies, and Amsterdam for derivatives.
This was then followed on 3 May 2000 by a proposed merger between the London Stock Exchange and Deutsche
Börse in which London would be the market for all major stocks and Frankfurt for all small, ‘high tech’ stocks. This
was to
                                       EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY                                               647


result in a market for established companies in London and for new companies in Frankfurt. Furthermore, this
London–Frankfurt merger involved an alliance with Nasdaq, which was also developing an operation in Tokyo, so
creating a global twenty-four-hour market. Subsequently, the New York Stock Exchange then linked to Euronext so
that it could also offer a continuous global market. However, the proposed London–Frankfurt link soon began to
unravel as reservations were expressed from those in the securities industry in both Britain and Germany. Financial
intermediaries in neither country were keen to see the markets in domestic securities being located in distant centres
operating unfamiliar rules and involving currency risks. This was especially so for the securities of smaller companies
that tended to be held by national investors and handled by retail brokers in Britain, and so looked for the familiarity of
a national market. The concept proposed by London and Frankfurt was perfect for an integrated European economy
operating under a single currency and a single set of ﬁscal and other policies, for then business could gravitate to
specialist markets, as in the United States. But that was not yet the case in Europe, making such a proposal both
speculative and hazardous. Consequently, even before the audacious bid from the Swedish O and M Stock Exchange
in August 2000, the London–Frankfurt merger had already begun to disintegrate as the details and complications
began to emerge. It was eventually abandoned in September 2000. What should now be clear to all is that the
refashioning of the global securities market is no easy matter, and that mergers between national stock exchanges with
long histories of separate development is not the same as mergers between companies, especially when national
governments continue to exert such a strong inﬂuence over their own economies. The European Union, for instance,
is not the United States of Europe, let alone the United States of America.
Even when converted into public companies, stock exchanges remained markets, and as long as their owners were also
largely the users of that market, their interest in its future went beyond the monetary value of their holding. Of far
greater consideration was the inﬂuence they could exert over the direction of that market, the quality of service
provided, the charges made, and the rules and regulations provided. For many this was of a national, not a global,
character. The requirements of integrated ﬁnancial institutions, with large-scale global operations and the ability to
internalize many market functions, were fundamentally different from specialist ﬁnancial intermediaries serving the
needs of private investors with largely static portfolios of domestic securities. The interests of both needed to be
accommodated if a marketplace was to be preserved that was both wide and deep, rather than narrow or shallow. In
the end, an organized market has to attract users if it is to survive and be successful, for these users could always
complete their business in other ways if the costs and restrictions drove them to do so. In the past, the result was an
evolving diversity of
648                                    EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY


stock exchanges, with each catering for different segments of the securities market.
Although the development of electronic trading networks has removed some of London's locational advantages, it has
also given it others, as business can more easily gravitate to the best market. Underlying London's advantages as a
centre for trading securities was the fact that the City of London was one of the major ﬁnancial centres in the world,
and so generated a vast amount of buying and selling activity in securities which was most easily and conveniently
undertaken within London itself. In addition to London's paramount position in the global money market, generating a
vast amount of activity in the securities markets, it was also a major investment centre. In 1999, for example, fund
managers based in London managed $2,500 billion of equity assets compared to $2,400 billion in New York, $2,100
billion in Tokyo, and $1,509 billion in Paris, Zurich, Amsterdam, and Frankfurt combined. With a large proportion of
these assets being managed from a London base by foreign banks and brokers on behalf of foreign institutions, this
made London the premier international market in the world. Consequently, of the London Stock Exchange's turnover
of £4,300 billion (to March 2000), 63 per cent was in international equities and only 37 per cent in the shares of British
companies. Even in the British shares, a substantial proportion of the turnover was driven from abroad, as 20 per cent
of UK equities was held by international investors, reﬂecting the global nature of Britain's largest companies.
Conversely, British institutional investors increasingly held foreign securities, as they searched for stable, long-term
growth for the funds they managed. The result was to make it difﬁcult for any other centre to match the breadth and
depth of the securities market available in London. Consequently, in July 2000, the Swiss Stock Exchange announced
plans to move its trading in the stocks of major companies to London, through a link with Trade-point. In fact, much
of the activity in many newer markets, such as those catering for ‘high tech’ stocks, was buoyed up by speculative
activity which, like the mining booms of the past, will leave in its wake insufﬁcient activity to justify their expenses. At
the same time, much of the trading on smaller stock exchanges was now dominated by one or two securities, making
them highly dependent on the fortunes of the company which had issued them. Though Vodafone accounted for 13.4
per cent of the capitalization of the London market in February 2000, Ericsson had reached 44.3 per cent of the
Swedish market.
Clearly, the future of both the London securities market and the London Stock Exchange no longer rested on the
demands of British investors, whether individual or institutional, but upon the place it could command in the global
securities market in terms of the securities it traded and the intermediaries it used. This was especially so because the
British securities market was relatively mature with around sixteen million individual
                                        EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY                                                649


investors and pension fund assets of $1,241 billion ($21,000 per capita) in 1999. In contrast, the habit of investing in
securities, especially with the aim of providing for retirement, remained relatively underdeveloped in much of
continental Europe, despite the pressing need to make such provision. In 1999, pension fund assets were only $286
billion ($3,500 per capita) in Germany, $195 billion ($4,300) in Italy, and $95 billion ($1,600) in France, indicating a vast
potential market for the issue and subsequent trading of securities as these countries moved from retirement schemes
ﬁnanced out of current income to ones based on long-term assets. As a result, the squabbles over winners and losers
among Europe's stock exchanges, which assume that the gains of one are at the expense of the others, are based on a
rather static picture of the future. Much more likely is a future where transferable securities—both equities and
bonds—comprise a growing share of ﬁnancial assets, so generating activity for stock exchanges of all kinds. From the
perspective of both companies seeking ﬁnance and investors—individual and institutional—seeking to employ their
savings, the securities market as a whole can look forward to a future where its facilities are in greater and greater
demand, so creating openings for different types of markets.
Whereas the London Stock Exchange may very well continue to be an attractive market for the securities issued by
major companies, as it responds to their needs and those of major ﬁnancial institutions, one consequence could be that
is does not adequately cater for either smaller companies or particular groups of securities such as ‘high tech’ stocks
and ones with only a regional following. If that was the case, the result would be a demand for the facilities provided by
other stock exchanges either in Britain or abroad, or via electronic trading networks provided by ﬁrms such as Reuters.
It is already clear that while London attracts the securities of the world's largest companies, it is losing those of smaller
British companies as the securities market changes in nature and form, for many have chosen to go private. Investor
horizons are no longer restricted by national boundaries and that has profound implications for the organization of the
global securities market and London's place within it. Fund managers, for example, tend to focus on the largest
companies, leaving smaller concerns somewhat neglected. At the same time, the tax advantages of a public ﬂotation
have largely disappeared. If the London Stock Exchange recognizes that its strengths lie in the international sphere and
then capitalizes on that by meeting the needs of the world's major companies and the world's leading institutional
investors, then it can recapture in the twenty-ﬁrst century the dominance it possessed at the beginning of the twentieth.
Otherwise it will become relegated to occupying a regional dimension to an evolving global securities market whose
centre lies either elsewhere or nowhere, with serious implications for the City of London as a ﬁnancial centre. It would
seem perverse for the London Stock Exchange to turn its
650                                    EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY


back on this global market—for it is the best-positioned of all major stock exchanges to capture it—in order to meet
the needs of small companies and retail investors in Britain. If the London Stock Exchange does not meet the needs of
these investors, there are plenty of others who will, given the open and competitive nature of the securities market
today. The OM Group's bid for the London Stock Exchange reﬂected their realization of the global opportunities
available in London for the technology and software they had developed for the Swedish securities market. What
appears unlikely is that the London Stock Exchange can meet the needs of all potential users.
Given the complexities of arranging mergers between established stock exchanges and the fundamental differences
that exist between national ﬁnancial and monetary systems even within an integrated Europe, it seems clear that the
London Stock Exchange should play to its own strengths. From that perspective it would appear easier for it to attract
securities business to London, through the existing network of banks and brokerage houses already located there,
rather than to try to redistribute the available business among the existing stock exchanges in some equitable manner.
The world within which the London Stock Exchange now operates is a highly competitive one and fundamentally
different from that which led to the merger of London with the other British stock exchanges in 1973. That was an era
when a merger between competing stock exchanges gave it a monopoly over the national market because of exchange
controls and regulations. However, that ended in 1979. What exists now is more akin to the pre-1914 environment
which saw the London Stock Exchange ﬂourish by attracting business from around the world through its combination
of a liberal attitude towards both new users and new securities, a reluctance to impose overly restrictive regulations or
burdensome charges, and a willingness to respond to changes in the environment within which it operated. All that was
driven by a realization that the Stock Exchange was not immune from competition at home and abroad, for the pre-
1914 world was both one of enormous and profound changes in communications technology, with the telegraph and
the telephone, and one where government largely left markets alone. In many ways the challenge facing the Stock
Exchange then was a simpler one than today, for the level of regulatory control then imposed upon it by government
was almost non-existent. To be successful in the twenty-ﬁrst century, the London Stock Exchange will have to serve,
simultaneously, two masters—namely the needs of the British government inﬂuenced by EU requirements, and the
needs of the securities market, driven by both global and domestic considerations. Whether it is possible for any single
organization to meet this challenge satisfactorily has to be doubted, and one of the tasks facing the London Stock
Exchange is to decide what function it does want to fulﬁl and then focus on that, to the exclusion of all others and
regardless of the criticism received from either
                                       EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY                                               651


the media or politicians, because that will exist whatever it does. The London Stock Exchange has had to reinvent itself
time and again to survive, and the present is no different from the past, although the urgency is more acute.
Above all, the London Stock Exchange has to determine the nature and level of the value added it brings to a securities
market. A stock exchange is, and always has been, different from a securities market, as it can deliver beneﬁts to its
users that they value highly. Even at a basic order-matching level, where buyers and sellers are brought into direct
contact with each other, there always exists the problem of counter-party risk where securities traded are not delivered
or paid for, creating problems and complications for all concerned. That alone requires rules and regulations to ensure
that any deal made is enforced and defaulters are excluded from future participation. Consequently, a stock exchange
adds value by introducing certainty to a transaction. It is not simply an electronic communication network—vital as
that is—available to all who care to use it, although many saw it as no more than that. Obviously, there are different
ways of guaranteeing certainty, whether through a code of conduct or by establishing a central counter party which
stood between users. Whatever the solution adopted, a stock exchange has to offer the certainty of completion for
every transaction if it is to establish a role for itself in the marketplace. Furthermore, the greater and more complex the
business being conducted, the more the stock exchange needed to respond to the needs of users searching, for
example, for a market in which securities could always be bought and sold instead of waiting until a perfect match was
found for their requirements.
The fact that securities alone possessed a ready market, unlike other assets, was one of the main reasons for their
popularity. That was the result of the existence of specialist intermediaries to undertake the business, a trading forum
where they could come together, and an environment that facilitated risk-taking by those who bought what they could
not pay for and who sold what they did not own, in the expectation of either reversing the deal or completing it
through borrowing in the wider ﬁnancial community. To this end, the London Stock Exchange may need to consider
what future structure it should adopt so that it is able to house both an electronic communication network and a
regulatory regime for intermediaries. The former provides the trading system, while the latter provides the orderly
market, and it is the combination of the two that represents the value added by the London Stock Exchange to the
securities market. However, both functions may not ﬁt a business enterprise whose purpose is to generate proﬁts for
its shareholders. Instead, a more suitable structure could be one where the provision and maintenance of the electronic
network is ﬁnanced through a charge on usage, whereas the administrative costs of regulation come from a
membership fee, with only those accepted as
652                                   EPILOGUE: TOWARDS A THIRD CENTURY


members able to trade on the network. Inevitably it will take time for the perfect formula to be found, but if—or
when—it is, the London Stock Exchange will enter upon that cycle where the very success of the market it provides
attracts more and more users, both in terms of corporate securities to be traded and ﬁnancial intermediaries wishing to
buy and sell on their own account or for clients. Difﬁcult as this task may appear, it is no more than the London Stock
Exchange achieved for most of its existence, when it was driven by the need to make a proﬁt for the proprietors of the
building in which it operated and to respond to the needs of those who used it to buy and sell securities.
Ranald C. Michie Durham
Durham
I November 2000
                                     Select Bibliography
Primary Sources
This book rests upon a careful reading of the records generated by the London Stock Exchange as an institution. The
main series used were:
  1.    Committee for General Purposes, 1798–1946
  2.    Committee of the Trustees and Managers, 1801–1948
  3.    Council of the London Stock Exchange, 1944–88
The minutes of the two Committees and that of the Council up to 1954, are lodged in the Guildhall Library, London.
The Council Minutes for the period after 1954 are still retained by the London Stock Exchange. Associated with the
Committees were numerous subcommittees whose records are also held by the Guildhall Library, and they were also
consulted. However, I did not consult the records of the even more numerous Council subcommittees, held by the
Stock Exchange, because of the vast increase in the volume of material included in the Council Minutes until the mid-
1970s. All subcommittees reported to either General Purposes or Trustees and Managers Committees, and later to
Council, submitting both reports and recommendations as well as supplementary papers, correspondence, and
opinions.
For the post-war, and especially contemporary, history of the Stock Exchange the following were also invaluable.
  4.   Annual Reports, 1956–97
  5.   Financial Times, 1983–2000
  6.    Stock Exchange Quarterly (became Quality of Markets Review), 1984–95.
(Detailed references are to be found in the footnotes.)
In addition, the Stock Exchange Ofﬁcial Intelligence/Stock Exchange Yearbook and Stock Exchange Factbook were invaluable
sources of statistical data.


Secondary Sources
Much of my already published work has been on stock exchange history, including that of the London Stock
Exchange, or was concerned with the City of London, or ﬁnance and investment. Thus, I have not included in this
bibliography references to contemporary and historical works which have been extensively used for my earlier writing.
Instead, this selective bibliography lists those books and articles that have been of most use in writing this history.
